questions.enonce_markdown:
Define the following terms.

(i) Excretion.

(ii) Homeostasis. *(4,5 marks)*
questions.corrige_markdown:
(i) **Excretion** is the removal from the body of the **waste products of metabolism** (and of substances in excess), such as urea, carbon dioxide and excess water and salts. These are toxic or useless if they accumulate. Organs of excretion: kidneys (urea, water, salts), lungs (carbon dioxide, water vapour), skin (sweat: water, salts, a little urea).

(ii) **Homeostasis** is the **maintenance of a constant internal environment** of the body (for example body temperature, blood sugar level, water and salt content, pH of the blood) within narrow limits, in spite of changes in the external environment. It works by **negative feedback**: a change is detected, then a response brings the factor back to its normal value.

questions.enonce_markdown: Describe the role of the kidney in osmoregulation. *(6 marks)*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Osmoregulation** is the control of the **water and salt content (osmotic pressure) of the blood and body fluids**. The kidney does it by changing the volume and concentration of the urine.

1. **Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus** monitor the osmotic pressure (water potential) of the blood.
2. **When the body loses water** (sweating, little drinking, salty food), the blood becomes too concentrated. The hypothalamus stimulates the **posterior pituitary gland** to release more **ADH (antidiuretic hormone)**.
3. ADH is carried by the blood to the kidney and makes the walls of the **distal convoluted tubule and the collecting duct more permeable to water**.
4. **More water is reabsorbed** into the blood, so a **small volume of concentrated (dark) urine** is produced and the blood becomes more dilute.
5. **When the body has too much water** (a lot of drinking), the blood is too dilute. Less ADH is released, the tubules become **less permeable**, little water is reabsorbed and a **large volume of dilute (pale) urine** is produced.
6. The kidney also **reabsorbs useful salts selectively** (and excretes the excess), so that the salt concentration of the blood stays constant.

The process is a **negative feedback**: the blood returns to its normal concentration.

questions.enonce_markdown: Explain how the human body regulates the amount of sugar level in blood. *(5 marks)*
questions.corrige_markdown:
The blood glucose level (about 90 mg per 100 cm$^3$) is regulated by the **pancreas** (islets of Langerhans), the **liver** and two hormones, **insulin** and **glucagon**, acting by negative feedback.

- **After a meal, blood sugar rises.** The **beta cells** of the islets of Langerhans secrete **insulin**. Insulin makes the **liver convert excess glucose into glycogen** (stored in the liver and muscles) and makes body cells **absorb and oxidise more glucose**; some glucose is converted to fat. Blood sugar falls back to normal.
- **When blood sugar falls** (fasting, exercise), the **alpha cells** secrete **glucagon** (adrenaline also helps in stress). Glucagon makes the **liver convert glycogen back into glucose**, which is released into the blood. Blood sugar rises back to normal.
- If the pancreas does not produce enough insulin, the blood sugar stays too high: **diabetes mellitus**.
